name: Permissions

hero.title: Downgrade the plan. The Export button hides itself.
hero.lede: Roles, ownership rules, feature flags and plan tiers behind one reactive function, `can()`. A rule that reads a signal re-checks when the signal changes, so every button, route and menu that asked follows on its own.

facts.value: 1.3–1.9× on the resolver race<small>One run, bun/JavaScriptCore, author-run. Exact deny ties.</small>
`posts.*` · `posts.**` · `*`<small>Most specific wins, so a deny beats a broad grant.</small>

why.title: Access rules that keep up with the user.

items.title: Rules that read signals re-check by themselves
items.text: `'posts.update': (post) => post.authorId === me().id`. Switch accounts with `me.set(…)` and every `can('posts.update', post)` on screen re-evaluates. Nothing to rebuild, no `ability.update(rules)`.

items.title: One shape for every model
items.text: Role grants are booleans, ownership is a predicate, a feature flag is `() => flags().beta`, a plan tier is `() => plan() === 'pro'`. All of them are string keys you check the same way.

items.title: Wildcards with a clear winner
items.text: `billing.**` grants the subtree, `billing.refunds.**: false` carves out refunds. Lookups go exact, then `*`, then `**`, most specific first, so the deny wins.

items.title: Fails closed
items.text: A predicate that throws, or returns anything other than `true`, denies. `can.assert()` throws `[Pyreon] permission denied: 'posts.delete'` for loaders and server actions.

difference.title: Stop rebuilding the ability on every login.

before.label: CASL 7
before.caption: An ability object built from the user. When the user or plan changes, you build it again and push the rules in.

after.label: with @pyreon/permissions
after.caption: The rule reads the signal. Change the signal and every check that depends on it re-runs.

comingFrom.title: Action and subject become one dotted key.
comingFrom.after:
<Show when={() => can('posts.update', post)}>
  <button>Edit</button>
</Show>

can.assert('posts.delete')
// throws "[Pyreon] permission denied: 'posts.delete'"
comingFrom.note: The models differ: CASL matches (action, subject) pairs with MongoDB-style conditions; Pyreon checks dotted string keys, and a condition is a plain function. Conditions you wrote as `{ authorId: user.id }` become `(post) => post.authorId === me().id`.

items.name: `can(key, context?)`
items.text: Reactive in JSX, `computed` and `effect`; pass the post, the team or the order as context.

items.name: `can.not(key)`
items.text: The inverse, for "show the upgrade banner".

items.name: `can.all(…)` / `can.any(…)`
items.text: AND and OR over several keys, with one shared context.

items.name: `can.assert(key, ctx?, msg?)`
items.text: Throws a `[Pyreon]` error on deny, for loaders, guards and server actions.

items.name: `can.set(map)`
items.text: Replace every rule after login, in one batch.

items.name: `can.patch(map)`
items.text: Merge a few rules when the plan changes.

items.name: `can.granted` / `can.entries`
items.text: Computed lists of what is granted, for a settings page or a debug panel.

items.name: `<PermissionsProvider>`
items.text: One instance per request on the server, one per test.

items.name: `usePermissions(['posts.edit'])`
items.text: A self-contained instance from a list of grants, for a story or a test, no provider needed.

recipes.title: Plan tiers as rules
recipes.text: The rule reads the plan signal. Upgrade, and the CSV export appears without a reload.

recipes.title: Grant a subtree, carve out one branch
recipes.text: Finance can do everything under billing except issue refunds. The more specific deny wins.
recipes.code:
can.set({
  'billing.**': true,
  'billing.refunds.**': false,
  'admin.*': true,
  'admin.users': false,
})

can('billing.invoices.export') // true
can('billing.refunds.issue')   // false
can('admin.settings')          // true
can('admin.users')             // false
can('admin.users.edit')        // false: '*' is one segment

limits.title: Hiding a button is not authorization
limits.text: Check again where the data lives: call `can.assert()` in the loader or server action, with rules built from the server's own session.

limits.title: One instance per request on the server
limits.text: Create the instance inside the request and pass it through `<PermissionsProvider>`, so two users never share rules during SSR.

limits.title: `*` is one segment
limits.text: `admin.*` matches `admin.users` but not `admin.users.edit`. Use `admin.**` for the whole subtree.

limits.title: Strings, not Mongo queries
limits.text: There is no condition language to serialize and send to a client. If your rules come from a database as CASL-style JSON, map them to keys and predicates once, at login.

faq.a: On the fair race, where both libraries resolve every check because the rule map holds one ownership predicate, 1.3–1.9× (one run, bun). An exact deny ties. The record also lists 2.7–13.8× for repeated checks of a static map, and says plainly that those are a cache read, not a race.

faq.q: Does a predicate re-run when the data it reads changes?
faq.a: Yes, when it reads signals. `can('posts.update', post)` inside JSX tracks whatever the predicate reads, `me()` included, and re-checks when it changes.

faq.q: How do I load rules after login?
faq.a: `can.set(rulesFor(user))` replaces the map in one batch, and every reactive check updates once. `can.clear()` on logout denies everything.

faq.q: Can I use it outside components?
faq.a: `createPermissions` is plain TypeScript: call `can()` in a route guard, a store action or a test without a provider.

related.name: Zero
related.text: Check `can.assert()` in loaders and server actions.

related.name: Feature
related.text: Put a `can()` check in front of the create, update and delete hooks it generates.

end.title: Who can do what, in one function your UI already listens to.

benchmarks.rival: vs @casl/ability 7 · bun/JavaScriptCore, one process per operation and library
benchmarks.h: 1.3–1.9× faster than CASL when both resolve.
benchmarks.p: Both libraries must return the same boolean for every check before timing. The race uses a rule map with one ownership predicate, which switches off Pyreon's memo the way a real app does, so both sides resolve every call. Exact deny is a tie.
